utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. The hearing was delayed due to technical difficulties. We will be sitting from 2.30 to 6.00. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Ms. Ruby Haazen, who is an environmentalist, a law graduate, a judo expert, and a sailing captain who's been assisting my team for the last three months. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, is there anything to raise? Otherwise, let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Excellencies. Good afternoon to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Gray.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D05523 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel Gray, did you provide the Defence a statement? Did you answer their questions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It appears on the screen to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you sign the statement as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I believe it was in April of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this statement accurate; i.e., does it accurately reflect what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and I wouldn't change a word of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I were to put the same questions to you today here in the courtroom, your answers would be the same, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender the 92 ter package into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D5523 will be Exhibit D2398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I come to the issue of the associated exhibits after you will have read out the summary of Mr. Gray's evidence for the public. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am going to read a summary in English. [In English] Colonel Richard Gray of New Zealand served as chief operations officer for the United Nations Military Observers programme in Sarajevo from April 1992 and senior military observer for Sector Sarajevo from June 11th, 1992, to September 20th, 1992. While in Sarajevo, he worked in United Nations Sarajevo Sector headquarters in the PTT building. He became aware that the Bosnian Muslim army used the workshop in the basement of the PTT building to manufacture and repair weapons. Colonel Gray stated that Army of BH snipers fired at the UN personnel at the PTT building from other buildings nearby, including the student hostel building. The United Nations made written protests to the Bosnian government about this. He was personally fired upon by the Bosnian government side on many occasions. Colonel Gray was also aware that the BH army also fired mortars from the immediate vicinity of the Kosevo hospital towards the Bosnian Serb positions in an attempt to draw return fire against a civilian facility. This was part of the overall strategy of the Bosnian government to obtain international intervention on their side of the civil war. He personally observed that the BH army parked the APCs just to the rear of the hospital under some trees. Colonel Gray also observed two BH army tanks parked 30 metres from the PTT building. They were deliberately using the UN headquarters as a shield from being attacked by the Bosnian Serbs. The BH army also had mobile mortars mounted in vehicles which they would drive to a position and fire towards Bosnian Serb positions. On July the 13th, 1992, mortars were fired at the PTT building killing and wounding a number of young people who were gathered nearby while the Canadian soldiers were throwing candy to them from the roof of the building. Colonel Gray believes that these mortars were fired by the BH army. Colonel Gray relates that it become routine for Bosnian government forces to shell their own area around the Presidency building whenever a foreign dignitary arrived. This occurred on 17th of July, 1992, when British foreign secretary Douglas Hurd visited the Presidency. On this occasion, ten bystanders were killed or wounded. Colonel Gray was present during this event and actually witnessed the mortar bombs exploding. He heard the primary charge from the mortar go off when he was in front of the Presidency. The mortars were fired from no more than 200 metres away. The mortar bombs had to come from the Presidency side. From his observations and experience in Sarajevo, Colonel Gray is convinced that the killing of their own citizens was also part of the strategy of the Bosnian government to obtain international intervention on their side of the civil war. Colonel Gray employed a group of translators from all ethnic backgrounds to translate the news being broadcasted on Sarajevo television as well as on the radio and in printed media. The news broadcasted on the Sarajevo television station contained inflammatory propaganda from the Bosnian government side against the Bosnian Serbs. He believed that the Bosnian government was using the TV station as a weapon of war and that it was a legitimate military target when shelled by the Bosnian Serbs. On 30th of June, 1992, pursuant to an agreement for the concentration of heavy weapons signed by Professor Koljevic, he developed [sic] half of the military observers, 30 of them, to the Serb side and the remaining observers, 30 of them, were deployed to the next day. While engaged in this assignment, he and his men were shot at by the Bosnian government side. Five UN personnel were wounded in the incident. In August 1992, Colonel Gray had one meeting with Dr. Karadzic and two with Mladic. These meetings were directed at reaching an agreement of the concentration of all heavy weapons in and around Sarajevo. Karadzic was the senior figure of the two. Karadzic did the talking but deferred to Mladic concerning matters of military practicality and the military realities. Colonel Gray found Dr. Karadzic to be sincerely interested in stopping the fighting in Sarajevo and in avoiding civilian casualties while the war was going on. Dr. Karadzic allowed Colonel Gray to visit and speak with the commanders on artillery and mortar positions thus far not under UN observation. General Mladic's diary accurately records Colonel Gray saying -- as saying at a meeting on August the 18th, 1992, that the Serbs had not initiated fire but returned fire for the past two months and that the Muslims were seeking international intervention and killing their own people. Even after the signing of the August 1992 agreement, the Bosnian government continued to provoke incidents in Sarajevo. On August 25th, 1992, the Bosnian government side shot and killed a member of the Ukrainian Battalion at the Marsal Tito barracks. General Nambiar sent a protest letter to President Izetbegovic. On September the 9th, 1992, the Muslims attacked a UN humanitarian convoy in the area of the Sarajevo airport killing two French soldiers. General Nambiar sent a protest letter to President Izetbegovic. He also protested the wounding of five UNMOs who were stationed at Serb artillery positions which had not opened fire. On 3rd of December, 1992, a UN board of inquiry concluded that the Muslims were responsible for the attack on the French Battalion in September 1992 which killed two French soldiers and had failed to punish those responsible for the attack. Colonel Gray toured the Bosnian Serb military positions around Sarajevo. They had a huge amount of heavy artillery around the city but were outnumbered by the Bosnian government forces. They used artillery as a way to defend their positions and to disrupt the Bosnian government forces inside Sarajevo. Colonel Gray believes that this was a legitimate military tactic so long as the artillery was not employed to deliberately target civilians or to engage in the disproportionate use of force. Colonel Gray believes that there were occasions when the Bosnian Serbs deliberately fired upon civilians in Sarajevo and used disproportionate force with their artillery in response to Bosnian government attacks. The indiscriminate and disproportionate targeting of civilians by the Bosnian Serbs seemed random to him as opposed to a deliberate policy. With respect to sniping, virtually everyone in the former Yugoslavia had access to weapons and it was impossible to determine whether the sniping of civilians was the result of orders or people acting on their own initiative in a civil war. [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, at the moment I don't have any questions for this witness, so I would like to hand over to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us deal with the associated exhibits. First, you are tendering the excerpt of the book by General MacKenzie: "Peace Keeper." Mr. Robinson, given that the relevant portion is fully cited in para 30, I don't think it's necessary or relevant to admit that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any objections, Mr. Costi, in relation to the remaining documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I'll just refer to the 65 ter numbers, 1D4891 and 1D5033. Given that the relevant portion is cited in their relevant paragraphs, I'm not sure whether they are necessary or relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that you're applying a different standard than you did to the Prosecution. It's one thing for a witness to say, I received this commendation, but it's another thing for you to see it and have him corroborate his statement. So with those, I stand by our request that those be admitted as associated exhibits and I don't see any -- I can't recall any instance in which a Prosecution document which had been referred to by the witness was excluded for the reason that it was duplicative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I didn't mean that they are duplicative, but the Chamber was just simply wondering if they are relevant to this case. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive them. The numbers will be given in due course. Mr. -- Colonel Gray, as you have noted, now that your evidence in chief had been admitted in the form of writing in lieu of your oral testimony, now you will be further cross-examined by the Prosecution team. Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gray. First of all, I want to thank you for agreeing to meet with the Prosecution, with myself and a colleague of mine, yesterday afternoon in the presence of Mr. Robinson. Second, I want to remind you, although you've already testified before this Court, that we have translation, simultaneous translation, going on. So you need to make the maximum effort to speak slowly and to pause between question and answers. So if you keep an eye on the record in front of you, you will realise when the typing is finished it's time for you to answer the question. First of all, I would like to touch upon some of the issues that we discussed yesterday afternoon. Paragraph 22 of your statement you said that: "Indiscriminate and disproportionate targeting of civilians by the Bosnian Serbs seemed random to me." And as you might recall we discussed yesterday because I asked you to explain me what did you mean by "random." And you told me that by "random" you meant that it was not a concerted effort to destroy a particular object, a particular target; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were explaining this "random" concept, you said that by contrast there were incidents where it was clear that the Serb forces were targeting a specific object. And you gave a few examples. And first of all, you mentioned the national library; isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Second, you mentioned the deliberate targeting of the gas bottling plant that supplies gas bottle -- bottled propane for the city. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: That is correct. It was the main gas bottling plant. People went there to get the propane to cook with --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: -- and, yes, it was deliberately targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you saw it yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: I saw it from the roof of the PTT and it was at night and it was like Guy Fawkes night.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And when talking about this incident you said that it was done to bring the civilian population to its knees. It was part of a sort of a psychological warfare; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: That is correct. The national library as an icon in the city and with so much history was done deliberately to reduce morale, I would think. I mean, that was my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: And in the same way that targeting the gas bottling plant, it was designed to reduce morale as well so that -- I mean, people had to start cutting down trees to actually cook.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also mentioned that the electricity in Sarajevo was going on and off. And if I'm not wrong you said it was like somebody was playing with the switch, and you said it was part of the same strategy.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: I didn't honestly know who controlled the electricity supply, but it was -- it was extremely annoying for everybody, not only the UN headquarters because we relied on -- obviously on electricity for our radios and various other pieces of equipment, facsimile machines and so on and so forth. So when the power went off usually the telephone lines also went dead because they have a small supply of electricity going through them. So it was hugely annoying. For the civilian population it was obviously far more severe.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 1D04892, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you will see up here on your screen one document that it was shown to you by the Defence and that you comment upon in your statement and your comment is at paragraph 35. It's -- it is one -- I'm sorry -- yeah, here we are. This is part of one article that was published in the New York Times on the 31st of July, 1992. And you are quoted saying - and you see in the third paragraph, if I'm not wrong, third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It says: "'They could destroy the whole city,' the Colonel said, 'they have enough firepower out there to flatten the city 10 times over, but they don't want to.' "And then he added," and it's again referred to you, "that he had spoken with Serbian troops at the hillside gun positions." And it is a quotation again, "'They don't want a war.'" Is it accurate -- accurate record of what you said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: The media often will take poetic licence, and I certainly was never interviewed by this particular person who wrote this article. And so it may have been -- my comments may have been taken out of context which happened to me quite a few times in the course of my duty with the UN and which for me was intensely annoying because comments would -- that the newspaper columnist or whoever will take a little bit here and a little bit there and string them together and miss out the bit in between which actually connects them together. So I don't believe that is -- the comment about they could flatten the city ten times over is totally correct and I will stand by that because I -- I saw the weapons with my own eyes and some of whom were manned by boys and old men. That may have been a point where I said they don't want a war because they weren't professional JNA troops and a lot of weapons I saw --sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: You -- you were talking about context. This is -- this is -- this is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 24058.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you will see appear on the screen the full article. Now, attached to your statement that is only the page that we just discussed, but, in fact, that was only the second page of the article. I still don't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm being told that it hasn't been released yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me consult with my Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Apparently we have some technical issues, so it's not a perfect day for technicalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So let me move on to another topic and then we get back to this one. Now at paragraph 34 of your statement you -- you talk about this meeting, that was also mentioned by Mr. Karadzic this morning -- right now in this summary on the 18th of August. And at paragraph 34 you are -- you confirm that it is accurate what you are reported to have said in the Mladic diary, meaning that the Serbs had not initiated fire in the past two months, in the prior two months. Now, you met with Mr. Siber, the deputy -- the deputy commander of the ABiH, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 24037A. Okay. We do have this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, Siber kept a diary and he published then a book which is called "War Diaries," and this is an extract from that book. And the entry for the 29th of July reads as the following and I'm reading for the record: "Karic and I meet with Colonel Gray again. I can see that the good man, Colonel Gray, find himself caught in the middle. The aggressor Serbs are lying to him, they are deceiving him, which me admits, and at one moment he says," and you said, "'I know they are lying when they say they are only returning fire. We can see that and we report on that.'" And then he continues. On the one hand we have the Mladic diary that suggested he was said that they never returned fire in the period of time, and on the other you have this record of this meeting where you are reported to having said, No, I knew that they were firing not in return. So my question for you is: Do you stand with the proposition that you are -- that in the two months prior to the 18th of August they never returned fire -- sorry, they only returned fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: I make the point to start off with that this is the first time I've seen this. I've never seen this before, and I wasn't aware that -- my dealings with Colonel Siber were extremely difficult. And I wasn't aware he was keeping a diary just as he probably wasn't aware I was keeping a diary. But we -- I stand by my statement here, and there is an inaccuracy in what General Mladic recorded. The very last line I think it says that I will be giving 200 observers to implement the third agreement. That is wrong. That is a bit of poetry there. I never said 200 observers. I mentioned a figure of 100. In fact, my plan required 105 military observers. Once I had toured all the gun positions both in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo -- but Colonel Siber was an extremely difficult person to deal with, understandably, because he was doing his very best for the Presidency forces as was Professor Koljevic for the Serb forces. And one thing that Colonel Siber is totally correct on is, yes, I was caught right in the middle. And I -- but I -- to lend a little bit of credence to my comment to General Mladic, I -- we found it very hard to determine who was firing first. And besides the initial five weapon concentration areas for the Presidency and the five weapon concentration areas for the Serbs, when it was not clear who was firing first and who was firing back, I went and I established observation posts which were not part of the agreement; they're what I did to determine who fired first and who fired back. And that is -- and after a period of experience by my military observers, they could -- and the positioning of the observation posts, they could quite accurately tell who fired first and then who fired back.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be grateful if a pause could be made between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It's partly my fault. So if I properly understand what you said, it was extremely difficult to establish who fired first? So is it correct that you cannot say hundred per cent for sure that in these two months the Serbs only returned fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: You are correct. I -- a hundred per cent, no, but 85 per cent, pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in any event let's talk about return fire. And if we look at the fire that was going out of the city from the ABiH forces and the fire going into the city from the Serb side, inside -- from the Serb side around the city into the city, the fire response was a lot heavier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: That is very correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And it was disproportionate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was -- if I can -- it was a matter of who had the most weapons and the most ammunition, and it was clearly that the Serbs had more weapons and more ammunition, and so - and I think I mentioned this to you yesterday - the -- if the ABiH were to fire, say, six mortar rounds out of the city into Serb positions, the Serbs may well fire back 30, 40, or 50 rounds. And so it was -- it wasn't six for six. It was disproportionate and that's what I called disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now - and this brings me to probably the last issue unless we are capable to go back to the one that we abandoned before - at paragraph 13 of your statement you talk about this incident that took place on the 13th of July when several rounds of mortar hit the PTT building and in particular they killed a group of teenagers that were gathered there on the street. And you said that you ran to try to save them, but -- but -- but unfortunately one young teenage girl died. Isn't it true, Mr. Gray, though that at that time you could not determine the source of the fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: It was extremely hard to determine. I had -- I had artillery and mortar officers who were working for me who were experts in crater analysis, and because of the irregular front line, it wasn't just a straight line, I mean it went around suburbs and so on and so forth. We knew basically who was on which side of the line. But when my artillery and my mortar officer -- my mortar officer particularly because there were 82-millimetre mortars and the closest one to the PTT building landed 2 metres away or 6 feet. And they did an examination of the mortar craters and using their compass and the technology that we had available to us and their experience they drew a line from where the mortar rounds impacted and from the direction that those mortars must have come from. And it -- my recollection is that it went through Bosnian -- Muslim position, then through a Serb-controlled area, into a Bosnian area, then into a Serb area. And they drew the line to the full extent of that -- that weapon is able to fire from.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So it is correct that you could not establish the source of the fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: We could not, but the -- I'm sorry, the accuracy with which those bombs landed, we determined meant that it was more likely that they had been fired from a shorter range rather than a longer range. And also, where the -- where the teenagers were at the very base of the PTT building, directly opposite in terms of geography, directly opposite the PTT building, there are apartment blocks which are quite high. So in order to actually observe those teenagers getting candy from the Canadians, you would be actually have to be able to see them at the base of the building. And it was our assessment that there was no Serb position that where they would have line of sight to actually see those teenagers at the base of the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter number 23053.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gray, this is -- I don't know if it has appeared already on your screen. I need page -- I need page 14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not released again, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. They told me I can go back to the other issue and meanwhile --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So we pause on this again and we were discussing about this "New York Times" article and I was asking 65 ter 24058. Now, as I was saying this is the -- yeah. This is the first part of the article that you were shown by the Defence. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Okay. So this is the context. If you go to the fifth paragraph from the bottom, the one that starts with "on Wednesday," you will see that it says: "On Wednesday night, the night sky over Sarajevo was lighted up by the heaviest shelling in weeks, so intense that residents returned anew to their basement bunkers where they had sheltered at an earlier stages of the siege." Do you recall this circumstance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm sorry, I don't see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It's "on Wednesday" -- if you count from the bottom --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: -- it's the fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It must have been the 29th of July because the article was on the 31st, which is a Friday -- which was a Friday, so the Wednesday must have been a 29th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I mean the two heaviest days of shelling and fighting were -- the first one was on the 14th of May and the second one was on the 8th of June, and thereafter that it was, I would call it, intermittent.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And if we go -- if you look at the last paragraph and when they start halfway through the last paragraph, it says: "... the overnight fighting was followed by an unusual alarm Thursday when the UN forces closed Sarajevo airport to the month-old relief airlift when pilots of incoming planes reported that they had detected Serbian radar in the hills around Sarajevo ..." If we can now switch to the next page, just realising that the second page properly -- yes, it is here. Perfect: "According to the United Nations, this violated the agreement under which the airport was reported ..." And then a little bit further down: "The incident caused new concern about Serbian intentions, but the New Zealander who is overseeing the radar operation, Colonel Richard Gray, argued vigorously with reporters over the responsibility of the Serbian forces for the continued fighting." And then there are these two passages that we discussed before --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: -- and that you discuss in your statement. So there was a general concern and a UN concern for the intention of the Serbs after a massive shelling that night and a violation of the open agreement, but still it appears that you vigorously argued that they did not want war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: The radars that you're talking about we were fairly certain were operated by Croatians and -- because the planes had to go over Croatian territory on their approach path to Sarajevo airport, and an Italian transport plane was actually shot down, it was a plane immediately after my one, and I was in an RAF transport plane which had all magic black boxes and things and could tell when it was locked onto by radar. And there was a lot of excitement in my aircraft that I was in when the RAF plane said, We've just been locked onto by radar and this was when we were miles out from the actual Sarajevo airport, clearly over Croatian territory. And the Italian plane which was immediately -- it was three minutes behind us in the landing cycle, that was shot down.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: This happened at the beginning of September, though --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: The -- we are talking about the end of July, and what I'm asking you is whether even if light of what happened that night and the general concern that you have read in the first page of the article, you argued and maintained that Bosnian Serbs wanted peace. utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: I think it is. I think it is. I mean, it's a -- as I said before -- I mean, I hadn't seen this before, and I mean how people can put such interpretations in the "New York Times" or -- I mean, I've never seen these articles before. And as I say, I mean, I know even from the New Zealand print media I was misreported on several occasions where they took things -- comments I made out of context and they didn't put in the piece -- the essential part for me and my integrity which actually connects the two statements together.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No, it's me. I keep making mistakes. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Just let me check whether I can go back to the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So I'm sorry for this going back and forth. So we were talking about the incident of the 13th of July, and I asked 65 ter number 23053. And if you look in paragraph 2 I believe it is discussing the incident we are talking about, and the conclusion at the paragraph is: "The mortar attack appears to have come from a southerly direction; however, the region has not been confirmed."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: That's correct. We couldn't determine because we -- as I said before -- sorry, am I going too fast? As I said before, when my mortar officer and my telegraph officer examined the craters and they drew a line with their compass on the map and they drew it on the map where the front line was. As I said, if you took it out to the furthest extent of the range of that particular weapon, it crossed from one to the other to the other, and we couldn't clearly say who fired it. But I also go back to the point that to actually have line of sight to these poor teenagers would have been extremely hard for the Serb side. But having said that, we did not make a judgement call on it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you cannot make it now either?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: No, no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I was told that it was not uploaded or released, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe we have done everything that was necessary, but perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

So that's an issue that was raised. Who wanted the war. That was raised by the article, the news article, that was put to the witness in the "New York Times." utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we did discuss the shelling and to that regard it's very appropriate to ask a question; we didn't touch upon any motive or -- by the Bosnians to draw fire to kill their own people. This wasn't touched in any -- in any way during my cross-examination.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, with regard to the contents of this letter of the 14th of July, written by General MacKenzie, how does this letter tally with what you yourself experienced and with the information that was available to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: It does to a large degree tally with what I personally observed in the visit by Douglas Hurd was -- I mean, I had been in Sarajevo since the 10th of April and I had my own suspicions for a long time, but the Douglas Hurd incident confirmed it for me beyond any doubt whatsoever that the Presidency forces were killing their own people for the media. When the Douglas Hurd incident happened, as has already been stated, I was standing on the front steps of the Presidency building no more than a hundred metres away from where the mortar bombs landed. There was a guard of honour which I believe was in my statement mounted by Bosnian police which lined one side of the road. There had been a disconnect in timings with Douglas Hurd. He had a meeting at the airport with Professor Koljevic first, then had a meeting at the PTT building, and I waited for him at the Presidency building for him to finish that meeting. Both sides were never given the full detail of timings or locations when a dignitary was visiting, to try and avoid what actually did happen. And usually what happened was that when the dignitary was in the Presidency building conducting his meeting with President Izetbegovic, then mortar bombs would land outside -- directly outside the Presidency building and that happened in all the cases where I attended with the dignitary, whether it was Douglas Hurd, Carrington, Goulding, or whoever. And it was a rather flippant comment that I made to General MacKenzie prior to going to the Presidency that would General MacKenzie want to bet on when the mortar bombs would land and he said to me in person, No, Richard, I won't. We know they're going to land. It is just a matter of when. Now, the honour guard of the Bosnian police moved away from the impact area prior to the mortar bombs landing. I had been talking to two ABiH officers on the front steps and they looked at their watch and they moved inside the Presidency building and closed the door behind them, leaving me standing by myself on the front steps and then the mortar bombs landed because the people who fired them had stuck to the original timings that they'd been told to fire those mortar bombs. And an ambulance appeared on the scene almost immediately and there were camera crews on the scene almost immediately to record the poor, wounded, and dead people. And that one incident proved beyond all possible doubt that the Presidency were killing their own people for the sake of the media, and I stand by that. Can I please add, I reported this -- I reported this to General MacKenzie and that -- and that was when he -- it was an internal thing and I didn't talk to the media about this, and it was General MacKenzie who then spoke to the media about it and that's -- shortly after that, he gave up his command of the UN headquarters in Sarajevo and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gray. The Chamber has a question for you. Judge Baird will put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to direct your mind back to the "Times" article and the reference that you argued and maintained that the Bosnian Serbs wanted peace, and you said this was a misrepresentation of your thought; is this correct? Am I correct there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I had never seen this article. I mean, I was in the middle of a war and I wasn't even aware of this article until I came here. And as I've said before, I have been misrepresented as saying things in my -- in the New Zealand media, my own media, if you like, and I know that I've been misrepresented in other media -- I mean, I was accused of being a war criminal myself and -- when I was in New York in 1993 by a tabloid press which was totally fatuous and totally untrue. And that is the sort of undue attention that UN officers who are just trying to do the very best that they could were treated like. I just go back to what I said before, that some of these comments are taken out of context and I certainly couldn't be attributed to saying some of these things. It's just someone making it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Colonel, in respect of return fire - and you gave an example of perhaps the Bosnian forces firing six rounds, six mortar rounds, and receiving 10, 20, 30, or more rounds in return and you describe that as disproportionate - plainly it would be disproportionate simply in numerical terms. Sometimes, however, in a military situation it might be necessary to neutralise a fire base by putting in a great deal of fire. Is that something you would consider a legitimate -- from your military experience a legitimate tactic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. In this particular situation I made reference in my statement that it wasn't a conventional war. It was a horrible civil war. And I had my military observers witness - and there are also other officers who witnessed it from the car-park at the Kosevo hospital right in front of the Kosevo hospital - where these mobile mortars that the Presidency had, they were in the back of a red van, one particular one, and they would go to the car-park and they'd fire off some mortar bombs from there and then they would move away, trying to draw fire against a hospital, which I couldn't countenance. But they did this around the city, not just from the hospital. They did it in other areas where -- which were clearly civilian areas. And the military reason for that was that they were mobile. They couldn't -- counter battery fire probably would not be able to get them, and they would have gone by the time any counter battery fire was directed at the source of the firing from the Presidency forces. So it was that -- so it wasn't a conventional war where you have a battery of mortars firing and then you have counter battery fire which is a traditional way of fighting a war. This was very untraditional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And just a supplementary question. How close to the mobile mortars that you described did you get in terms of physical distance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD GRAY
utterances.text: The -- my observers who actually saw this, the one, for instance, at the hospital car-park, the person who observed that being fired was no more than 20 metres away, and their roof was cut in -- I mean, a hole was cut in the roof of the van and from the side you -- it looked like an ordinary van, but then a mortar bomb would come out of this hole in the arrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and I'm sorry about this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular rule here at the Tribunal. When you say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the discretion to oblige you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read Colonel Simic's summary in English. [In English] Savo Simic joined the active service in the JNA upon completion of the military academy of land army in 1982. He was chief of the artillery of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. From late 1994 until the beginning of April 1995 he was commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps' 4th Mixed Anti-Armour Artillery Regiment, and from that date until the end of the war he was a desk officer in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command artillery organ. In 1991 they already had knowledge about monitoring activities and typical engineering works for configuring military positions on Mojmilo Brdo as well as about the formation and arming of Muslim paramilitary groups. From mid-1991 JNA forces were facing problems with manning in army personnel. In his unit in the Lukavica barracks there were still officers of all nationalities until March and April 1992, when non-Serbian officers started leaving the unit. The first attack on Lukavica barracks was from Mojmilo Brdo sometime in early April 1992. Men in the mixed artillery division were all people from the local villages who volunteered to join the unit. The large majority of them were not trained for duties on artillery weapons, so the unit was forced to train them for the certain specialties upon their arrival in the unit. From late June 1992, UNPROFOR monitors were deployed to all the artillery positions in the brigade. One monitor and an interpreter spent 24 hours at the division command post. They registered every instance of fire being opened and they always knew the type of target, its co-ordinates, and why it was being targeted. The main task of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was to protect Serbian ethnic territories in Sarajevo and its surroundings. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was mainly engaged in defensive operations. As far as Colonel Savo Simic can recall, the only offensive operation was conducted in 1993, the goal of which was to join the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Herzegovina Corps. Apart from this, other offensive actions were carried out to improve the tactical positions of their forces. This was the case of the operations for liberating part of the Vraca-Trebevic road and the attempt to liberate a part of Soping. His unit was commanded by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander and the VRS General Staff several times for its level -- high level of training and skills as well as commendable discipline. The forces of the 1st Corps of the BH army in co-ordinated actions with the forces outside the city tried to break out of Sarajevo throughout the war, which would have greatly affected the other fronts and the general course of the war in BH. They set up large-calibre artillery in the parks and other areas and set up mortars on roof-tops. They also had vehicles with mortars mounted on their cargo platforms which allowed them to change their firing positions quickly. Muslim forces had numerous military targets in civilian zones and engaged in several offensive operations in the period between 1992 and 1995. Neither he nor any members of his unit or superior commands ever had the intention of causing civilian casualties or terrorise civilians under the control of Muslim authorities. In those situations when his unit had to respond to the enemy fire, he would select the most precise weapon in order to avoid civilian casualties. Colonel Savo Simic saw modified air bombs for the first time in the second part of 1994 on the Nisici plateau. These weapons had built-in sighting mechanisms and this made it possible for weapons to be very precise and the crews manning these weapons were well-trained. Air bombs were used because they had them in stock and using them in a standard way they compensated for the lack of the classical artillery ammunition. Regarding the incident in Vase Miskina Street on 27th of May, 1992, in Savo Simic's opinion it is impossible to say with certainty the distance from which the shell was fired. In the Bistrik and Sirokaca sector there were some Muslim mortar firing positions which were used to attack Serbian positions and civilian buildings in Vraca and the Grbavica throughout the war. Regarding incidents in Dobrinja on 12th of July, 1993, and Alipasino Polje 22nd January, 1994, in the opinion of Colonel Savo Simic the shells were fired from the Butmir sector from positions under the control of the Muslim forces. Regarding incident in Oslobodilaca Sarajeva Street in Dobrinja on 4th of February, 1994, Colonel Savo Simic states that at that time all artillery weapons of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, including 120-millimetre mortars, were under the control of UNPROFOR. Regarding incidents in Safeta Zajke Street and Majdanska Street on 24th of May, 1995, Colonel Savo Simic responsibly claims that not a single modified air bomb was ever launched from the zone of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Regarding incident Markale I in 1994, Colonel Savo Simic states that it is not possible for someone to deliberately fire on the market and hit it in the first attempt. Adjusting fire would be needed. Regarding incident Markale II 1995, Savo Simic states that it is not possible to conduct adjusting fire from one position in order to hit the target from a different position. The adjusting fire has to come from the same position. Therefore, the fifth round in Markale II incident was another first attempt, like Markale I. I don't have any questions at this point in time, but could Colonel Simic be shown his statement in the Serbian language for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
