utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what was your rank in 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: In 1992 I was a captain first class. I was promoted to the rank of major at the beginning of 1994, in March or April, I believe. And I was a major until the end of the war. After the war I was promoted to lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you still in the military or have you left and what is your rank?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: It was on the 31st of December, 2007, that I retired with the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that we have clarified the matter on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Colonel Simic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. You will now be further cross-examined by the Prosecution. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But given the time, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 35 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Simic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by asking you some questions about how the corps, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and your particular brigade as well as the other brigades worked. By the way, sometimes you'll see me pausing. It's because I'm waiting for the translation to conclude and it's worth noting that if either one of us begin speaking too fast the interpreters will have difficulty keeping up. So it's useful to be reminded of that at the outset and perhaps periodically as we go through the examination. First, Colonel, was it required that the brigade submit reports to the corps on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was obligatory to send daily reports to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us how these reports from the brigades to the corps were compiled, how the brigades got the necessary information and what information it communicated to the corps?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Given that the brigade's command was located in the vicinity of the corps command, reports were sent by courier. The daily reports contained information on the situation in the battle-field during the day on ongoing activities, on whether attacks had been launched. The reports were compiled on the basis of reports received from subordinate units in the battalion commands. They also included information on whether there were any wounded or any men killed, whether the combat deployment had changed, about problems in the units, about logistics support, requests for fuel, ammunition, and so on and so forth, information on any possible shortcomings. They were the usual kinds of reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it would be the case, as I understand it then, that each of the subordinate units within the brigade had an obligation to report relevant information on up to their superiors so that there'd be a flow of information on a daily basis up to the brigade so it could report to the corps?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of the day, did the brigade also -- did the brigade receive both written reports and oral reports from its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it received information. If there was any combat the units would provide the information immediately. If any assistance was required the brigade command would be informed of the situation in the unit's depth and they would also phone and give oral reports. Written reports were also sent. If necessary, interim reports, written reports, could be sent. After the regular daily report had been sent, if there had been any important changes for the period in question, in such cases an interim report would be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And within the brigade, who was responsible for receiving and compiling information that would take the form of the report to the corps and who was responsible for authorising or approving the release of that information, that particular information, to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The duty operations officer would compile the report and take it to the brigade commander to sign it. He would be informed of the situation. After the brigade commander had signed the report, the report would then be sent to the corps command. Or if the brigade command was absent, then the officer replacing him would sign it, his deputy, or rather, the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that reports could also be sent after the regular report was sent. Was there a dead-line for the submission of the regular daily report?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Interim reports would, as a rule, be sent after the regular daily report if necessary. It was necessary to provide the corps command with information, but the daily report had already been sent. It wasn't at a definite point of time because we didn't know when certain things would happen, but if anything happened after the event and after having obtained the information the information would then be sent to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, that question may have been a bit confusing. Let me -- I wanted to focus on something slightly different. With respect to the interim reports, I presume that that mechanism was available not only for information that the brigade wanted to convey after the regular report, daily report, had been sent, but also if some unusual or extraordinary circumstance arose before the normal time for submission of the daily report; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And my earlier question was just trying to get an understanding of whether there was a particular dead-line or expected time by which the regular daily report would be sent every day?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, there was a dead-line for sending regular daily reports. They would be sent at a certain time so that the corps command could inform the Main Staff of the situation in its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall that time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, it was around 1400 or 1500 hours, but I can't claim that with certainty. So it included information on what had happened since the previous day, the previous report, and up until that point in time. It also depended on what the command thought was necessary and information was sent on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you've already alluded to, the corps command would then forward -- would then presumably compile all the relevant information from its brigades and send its own report to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Main Staff would then send a report to the supreme commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that sort of focuses on what would happen during the course of the day and at the end of the day. Were there also regular daily morning briefings about the tasks that were to be undertaken in the field by the subordinate units of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In the reports information was also provided on the tasks that had been assigned, on how the tasks were being carried out, to what extent they had been carried out, and also problems that had been encountered when carrying out the tasks. Assistance would be requested from the superior command if such assistance was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me focus for a moment on the aftermath of the submission of the reports on a particular day, and let me do that in the context of the corps and what you know about the operations of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from your experience. So the next day begins. Was there a regular morning briefing conducted by the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I was in the corps command from April, the beginning of April, 1994, until the end of the war; and common practice in all units and in the corps command was to have morning briefings, meetings with the corps command or the Chief of Staff. Tasks would then be assigned. The previous tasks would be analysed, as well as the problems that we faced. So that was common in all units, unless there was ongoing combat or it was impossible for the corps command to meet. In such cases there wouldn't be any such briefings. If the commanders and the Chief of Staff and the assistants were engaged, if they were in the field -- well, then we could meet or we might not be able to meet. But in normal circumstances, we'd meet every morning and the tasks would be assigned or the work carried out on the previous day would be analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And periodically, you say every week or two weeks, did the corps commander conduct briefings with the brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was an official in the artillery and I had my superior officer. That probably was the case, but as to the period concerned I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to the assistant commanders for the various sectors, such as security or logistics or morale, were there also independent units which were actually attached directly to the corps?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Which independent units do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, for example, as the mixed artillery regiment, the military police, the engineering battalion, and so on, were they directly within the corps?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean independent battalions, independent regiments. These units were independent units within the corps. They had their commander, their own establishment, and they reported directly to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the assistant commanders also reported directly to the commander, as you've already indicated; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Assistant commanders in a given area, professional area, that they were involved in would report on problems from their domain. The chief of engineers would report on issues that concerned him. The chief of artillery would report on his domain. The chief for logistics would report on his own area. They would inform the commander of any matters that were relevant and that he should be informed of. They tried to find solutions for certain problems, if there were any problems, and they tried to reach agreement on the activities that were to be pursued in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the assistant commanders - and let me use one assistant commander for the moment as an example - the assistant commander for security and intelligence, did that assistant also have a counterpart at the Main Staff level?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: He certainly did, but I'm not familiar with such things, with security and intelligence and the chain of command. He probably had a superior officer in the Main Staff. As to how they submitted reports, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then let's -- let me focus then on your particular area, and that is artillery. Did -- in addition to reporting to the corps commander -- well, did the chief of artillery for the corps also report to his counterpart in the Main Staff or was there -- first of all, was there a counterpart for the chief of artillery in the Main Staff, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so the -- and so my question then is: Did -- in addition to reporting, as you've described to the corps commander, did the chief of artillery for the corps also have a reporting channel and some level of subordination to the chief of artillery for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: He didn't submit any written reports. If it was necessary to report orally, he'd phone. If necessary, perhaps he wrote certain written requests or reports, but I'm not aware of that. But on the whole he reported orally. It wasn't his duty to write regular reports, written reports. This was done through the regular reports that were sent every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me focus for a moment then on your own particular reporting obligations and superior/subordinate relationships in the roles that you've described in your statement. During the period of time you were chief of artillery in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, to whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the brigade command. I personally didn't send reports. The command of the mixed artillery division did that. I was a member of the brigade. Circumstances would have it - as the President said in the summary - there was a problem when the unit was being brought up to strength with volunteers. At the beginning of the war, most of them, 90 per cent of them, weren’t from the artillery and I as the only professional -- or one of the few professional officers at the time when the Army of Yugoslavia left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I remained at the command post in that division in order to provide assistance with making the members of the unit professionals, turning them into professionals, training them. I remained there at that command post until the end of December, November or December, 1993, I believe. And as for the reports sent -- it was the command of the division who sent them to the command of the brigade. There wasn't a great distance between the command posts, so couriers were used to send reports and contact was established on a daily basis over the phone, and all important issues were discussed on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. In the transcript the witness said that 90 per cent of them did not have a military establishment position. Here it sounds as if they came from the artillery. So this has been wrongly interpreted and recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll ask the CLSS to take a look at this. Mr. Tieger, if I can interrupt this moment. You dealt with the role or the position of chief of artillery. Let's take the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Mr. Simic, there was a chief of artillery in the SRK, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could your repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. There was a chief of the artillery in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And he was a member of the staff of the corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, in case of chief of security, he's an assistant commander for security. Is he also a member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The assistant commander for security was the assistant commander, not in the staff. He was the assistant to the commander. He was directly under the commander, subordinated to the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you -- in the Sarajevo Corps there's two artillery regiment, one the mixed artillery regiment and the mixed anti-armour artillery regiment. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your understanding is good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain to us the relation between the commanders of those two regiments, the chief of artillery and the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The regiment commanders along the command lines were directly subordinated to the corps command. In professional terms they were subordinated to the chief of artillery in the corps. In other words, the chief of artillery is the professional body in the corps command when it comes to artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So the regiment -- those regiment commanders will report directly to the corps commander, but at the same time they'll make a professional report to the chief of artillery; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were in communication with the chief of artillery. In terms of professional issues, they took advice from him. They consulted with him on all those important issues pertaining to the area of artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I know the ranks at the time of the chief of artillery as well as the commanders of those two regiments, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of artillery -- at first, at the beginning of the war, all three of them were lieutenant-colonels. The chief of artillery in the corps, the regiment commanders, and sometime during the war - I don't know when exactly - they were promoted to the ranks of colonels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me follow-up on some of those questions, Colonel Simic. As chief of artillery in the 1st Mechanised Brigade, what were your general responsibilities? I know you already alluded to some of them in your previous answer, but I'd like to know your formal responsibilities as chief of artillery.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, I was supposed to take care of the professional training of the unit for combat tasks. I was not in charge of discipline. It was the battalion commander who was in charge of that and his subordinated commanders were -- reported to him on that. If there was any free time and there was no combat, I organised training so that my unit members were always active, they were always involved in training unless there was combat going on. My other tasks were to inform the brigade commander about the professional capabilities of the unit, the problems of logistics support - if there were any - in terms of artillery so as to make sure that the unit was at all times capable of performing its tasks. When it come to the issues of morale, discipline, and the situation in the unit, it was the commander of the battalion who was in charge of that and he was the one who reported on those issues. That would be in a nutshell. And moreover, in the brigade command I also provided my input on the use of artillery; i.e., I provided my proposal to the brigade commander. And the brigade commander at the end of the day decided whether to accept my proposals or not, or perhaps he had his own suggestions and he would issue orders as to how to place the artillery, how to deploy the assets. And then the orders were carried out. If a combat order was being drafted, I provided my input for the artillery use, both verbally and graphically, using a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And based on that input, assuming it was accepted, it would then be the commander who would issue the order to the subordinate units to -- for artillery use?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You alluded to your involvement in training unless there was combat going on. What was your role during combat?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: My role in combat was as follows: I was at the observation post together with the brigade commander in most cases, or I had my own observation post but then I was in direct communication with him. The brigade commander issued orders from the scene and I was briefed and updated on the situation in the zone of responsibility and about possible problems on various axes within the zone of our responsibility of the brigade in order to be able to react in due time when it came to the use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to what extent and how did your role change when you became a commander of the mixed anti-armour artillery regiment?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The role changed insofar that I was subordinated to the corps commander. I was no longer a member of the brigade. I reported directly to the corps commander. During the period that I spent in the mixed anti-armour artillery regiment, there were no missions. There was no combat. No fire was opened from our positions. Therefore, I spent most of my time at the observation post on the positions where it was necessary, mostly at Nisic plateau and Trnovo, which is where Muslim forces from Sarajevo in concert with units from elsewhere tried to breakthrough our lines. This is where I extended assistance to the brigade commanders pursuant to the orders of the corps commander. And very often, if not always, the corps commander was also there in the places where it was most -- where his presence was most necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to an artillery fire plan, you spoke earlier of your input to the brigade commander. In connection with that same issue as commander of the mixed anti-armour artillery regiment, what was your role or what was your anticipated role in the -- in devising artillery plans?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: My role was to act with the chief of artillery and to draft plans, but we didn't do that because it was not necessary because anti-armour regiment was not used, there was no need for its use, which is why my chief of artillery engaged it on those axes where it was more necessary to extend assistance to the brigades when it came to the stopping of breakthroughs and incursions and attacks of the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And now focusing on the period from April 1995 when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one clarification, Mr. Tieger, sorry. Who did you refer to when you said "my chief of artillery"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant my superior, the chief of artillery from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I indicated I wanted now to focus on the third role that you identified in your statement and that was, as indicated in the statement, from April 1995 until the end of the war when you were - it says in your statement - a desk officer in the SRK command artillery organ. What were your responsibilities as -- in this position?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I was assistant commander of artillery. I was his desk officer and I carried out his orders and his tasks concerning artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what did that involve in terms of your -- both your daily role in either receiving information from subordinate units, drafting plans, and so on? And then I want to ask you after that what it involved in terms of specific operations that were envisioned or carried out?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Together with the chief of artillery, I worked on the plan of use of artillery. The chief of artillery made proposals; I assisted him. He would draw the plan of action on the map. And pursuant to the order of the corps commander, we would do excerpts from that plan. That's when it came to combat. And pursuant to the orders of the chief of artillery, if he would send me to one of the corps units, I would go, inspect, and extend assistance if I encountered any problems. I carried out his tasks and orders in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How extensive was this reach-out to the subordinate commands, that is, going into the field to find out what the subordinate commands -- the subordinate units were doing, whether they had any problems, the extent to which they were implementing their tasks, and so on? How frequent was that? How regular? And who was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: When I was sent to forward command post of the corps from my observation post, I would communicate with the units in that area of responsibility, on that axis. However, at that same time I was also in communication with other units if they needed me, with the units that were not on that axis. However, my main task for which I was actually sent out was at the forward command post where I acted in concert with the chief of artillery and I assisted him with the use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the chief of artillery also go into the field and make direct contact with subordinate units to identify problems, check on implementation for all the issues that such contact might assist on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I correct the transcript. A very important element has not been recorded in the previous answer. The witness said that he observed the actions of the artillery on that particular axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had just asked you about the efforts of the chief of artillery in connection with going into the field, making direct contact with subordinate units to identify any problems, the extent of implementation of tasks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: At the forward command post we met with our artillery units, i.e., with the commanders on the axis where action was going on. We organised the use of artillery, we chose firing position, we decided how fire would be opened, and we observed artillery actions and we assisted artillery commanders in the performance of their combat tasks and orders. Likewise, if I may, we also observed and monitored the activity of the enemy artillery. We tried to establish their firing positions, to determine where they were firing from, and we provided information if we had them before the battery commanders where those firing positions were, and we gave them the tasks to neutralise the enemy artillery in those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I asked you about the chief of artillery. I should ask you this question as well: Did the corps commander also go into the field for the purpose of determining the extent to which orders were being implemented, tasks were being achieved, problems may have existed, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The zone of responsibility of the corps was extensive, it was large, and the corps commander would be where he was most needed. He was not there permanently, but he toured the theatre of war and he was kept well abreast of the situation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with your activities with the mechanised brigade, that is, the period of time when you were chief of artillery for the mechanised brigade, I think you referred in paragraph 19 of your statement to the fact that the unit was -- it says -- well, I may actually see if there's a small language correction needed. It says: "The unit was commanded," it says in English, "commanded by the SRK commander and the VRS Main Staff several times for its high level of training and skill and commendable discipline." I read that as probably actually saying that the unit was commended by the SRK commander and the VRS Main Staff, and I wanted to know if that's accurate or not? Again, that's paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it does say that the unit was commended for the high level of training, high level of discipline, and so on and so forth, by the commander of the SRK and the Main Staff and the brigade command, of course. The brigade command and the brigade commander have been omitted from the group, but they also commended the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification. There's a one-letter difference in the translation in English that changes it from the word "commended" to the word "commanded," and that's what I wanted to clarify. That would seem to suggest by its emphasis on the high level of training and discipline and so on that the unit or at least the commanders of the unit were not themselves reprimanded or disciplined or punished for any of their activities during the course of the period you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking if you can sit a little closer to the microphone so they can hear you more easily.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: There was no need to reprimand anybody or punish them because there was no lack of discipline. There were some minor problems like in any other unit or in any other institution where you work with people, but none of them mandated graver sentences or a more serious reprimand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to the extent you know it by virtue of your experience there, was that a remarkable situation for the brigades or was that situation, as you understood it, basically mirrored in the rest of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say anything about any of the other brigades. I don't know anything about them or about any other units of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. I don't know what the situation was there. I know about things that I was responsible for. I was not responsible for discipline, but I was concerned with that. Because for a unit to be superbly trained it had to show a certain level of discipline. I insisted on that from the beginning of the war, I cared about that; and finally it paid because we were prepared to perform all the tasks given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you got to the corps command it seemed -- I take it -- well, when you got to the corps command did you learn anything to the contrary about the other brigades, or as far as you knew at that time their performance was also deemed commendable or at least sufficiently commendable?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that there were commendations. I'm sure that all units of the SRK were serious. They performed serious tasks. They held very important positions. One can conclude that. I can't remember whether there were any commendations or not, but it can be concluded based on the actions of those units and soldiers what their dedication was and all the officers starting with the brigade commander to the last foot soldier, when the situation was serious and dangerous, when they were on their positions during combat, they proved their medals. So one can conclude that the situation on all units was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn, if I may, to a few different matters raised in your statement. First I noted that at paragraphs I think 4 through 7 you make some references to the difficulties that the JNA was having roughly from mid-1991 on with respect to maintaining personnel. And in paragraph 5 you attribute that to the recommendation -- or at least you attribute that in seemingly large part to the recommendation of the Muslim political leadership. And then you go on to describe the -- to some extent the pattern of departure of first, the recruits, and then the officers. Now, of course you were aware that at that time the JNA was involved in the or in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I presume you were aware at that time that this was a war about which many non-Serbs believed that the JNA had taken the side of Serbs against Croats in a quite bloody campaign involving attacks on Croats and Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The JNA did not take sides. In Slovenia and in Croatia the JNA tried --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I -- I think the Court will appreciate if I make clear that I'm not inviting you to explain your view of the JNA's position in that. My question was slightly different and that is whether you were aware that many non-Serbs believed that the JNA had taken sides and that the JNA was engaged in ethnic cleansing in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: My opinion - and I stand by it - is that the JNA did not participate in cleansing -- in ethnic cleansing. Up to the last moment, members of the JNA believed that there would be no war, that war would be stopped; however, their political leadership decided differently. And then under pressure they left the JNA, and obviously recruits and soldiers left units, and as soon as they did that sometimes they were even let go of their own will. But there were also those who remained because they believed in the JNA. They believed in the officers who were in charge, who were in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I understood from your statement your history with the JNA and I was not asking you to offer an opinion of your own against the JNA. But let's -- let me just be plain with you. It's got to be true, isn't it, that you knew about the views that many, many - if not the vast majority of Serbs --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this permissible? Can this be allowed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President, I am entitled to ask leading questions and that's precisely what I'm doing. And I am a little surprised about the intervention. I thought the accused was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: What was the ground of your objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection had nothing to do with leading questions, but the witness is being asked to speculate about what other people thought or believed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the answer -- the witness can -- the way he can answer to the question is yes or no. If he wasn't aware, he can say that he didn't know. Mr. Tieger was not asking the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Actually, I think the difficulty arose in that, Mr. Tieger, you weren't finished with your question, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Perhaps you can hear the question in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I -- thank you, thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm just trying to ask you a fairly straightforward question, but I'm kind of putting it in the form of a statement to which you can agree or not agree. You were aware, weren't you, that many, many non-Serbs, if not the vast majority of non-Serbs, were opposed to the war in Croatia and believed that the JNA had taken sides and that the JNA was engaged in a bloody campaign against Croats and they had those objections to the war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I know how the war unfolded in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, how it started. I also know members of other ethnicities who were part of my unit. Before the war when all had started in Croatia, I went from the garrison I was in, in Kiseljak, I was driven by a soldier, a Croat, who was providing security -- there was a policeman who was providing security, he was a Croat. And the unit was taken from one garrison to another, I went through Vinkovci, through Croatian settlements, and I trusted those soldiers and they trusted me. So as far as members of the military are concerned, well they are the persons I can discuss. Until the very last moment, they believed that the political leadership of those republics would reach an agreement, that they would make sure that there wouldn't be a war, and this is shown by the fact that many Croatian officers, Macedonians, Montenegrins, Hungarians were in the VRS and remained in the VRS until the end of the war. They did not leave it. And they had certain convictions. The JNA didn't take anyone's side. It strove to put an end to a bloody conflict; however, this did not suit everyone and what happened happened. And then it seems as if it's the GNA that took somebody's side. The JNA didn't have the intention of taking anyone's side. And as I said in my statement, the first attack was carried out from Mojmilo hill. It's item 8 of this statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, let me stop you. Normally I don't want to interrupt you but I think we're a little bit far afield. Let me ask you this question: Is it your testimony to this Court that the war in Croatia and the attitude of non-Serbs concerning that war did not play any significant role in the personnel problems that the JNA had from mid-1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The war in Croatia certainly started earlier on and the -- and recruits from the area of Croatia stopped joining units. Members of Croatian ethnicity in Bosnia, there were still Muslims, or rather, there were members of Muslim ethnicity in the units, but they were under constant pressure from the political leadership; and as a result, they stopped sending them to regular JNA units. Subsequently as we were faced with the problem of bringing units up to strength we started calling on the reserve forces; and in that case, Muslims from the reserve forces did not respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me move on to a related issue then. At paragraph 7 you relate an incident involving a Muslim non-commissioned officer who loaded up a truck and took weapons which were handed over to the Muslims, you say in the statement. Were you aware that in that general time-period, that is, the end of 1991 toward the first half of 1992 or the first quarter of 1992, that the JNA was providing -- JNA and the SDS were providing weapons to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. All I know is that we issued weapons to the reserve forces that responded to the call-up to join units. We issued weapons to them and that reserve force was under the command of the JNA unit they had been deployed in. That was also the case for volunteers who joined up after the war had already broken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbs received weapons from the JNA or the SDS, that is Serbs who were not part of the JNA or the TO structure?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that at the time when the war had already broken out I was a battery commander and I brought my unit up to strength with 30 or 40 men. I couldn't say exactly how many of them there were at the point -- at that point in time. These units were brought up to strength. First we called on the reserve forces, but since the process had been disrupted because the Muslims weren't coming and the war had broken out, we sought volunteers and brought the unit up to strength in that manner. We did that intensely when the JNA left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the 19th of May. And my unit, all my members, were issued weapons by me from the war time reserves that were intended for reserve units, but I'm not aware of what the situation was in the case of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to turn to page 14 of your -- paragraph 14, rather, of your statement. And there you say: "As far as I know, the SRK was surrounded doubly, internally and externally." And I wanted to look at a map and see if I could understand better what you meant by the claim that the -- it was the SRK which was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I could call up P01021, please. And if we could zoom in a bit on the circle to the left, and perhaps a bit more and stop us when ... all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, can you see that with sufficient clarity to make it out?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not on a very large scale, but I can see where these various units are deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And does that circle represent the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do we see the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps off to the right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it to a certain extent in the right lower corner. But if that's the area of responsibility, but I don't think it is. I can't see these features on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just tell us as you understand it what the dotted --

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as you understand it, what the dotted blue line represents and the dotted red lines and in what sense they indicate that the SRK is surrounded internally and externally?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The blue dotted line is in the defence line of the Muslim enemy forces. The dotted red line is the front line of defence of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska. It's quite clear here that everyone was encircling everyone else, or rather, everyone was semi-encircled. It wasn't a standard encirclement. You can see behind the rear of the 1st Sarajevo Romanija Brigade that you have enemy forces. That axis in the direction of Pale and Vlasenica was open, so there was a sort of semi-encirclement there, but I won't even mention troops at the front line who were under fire from their flank, from behind, from the front. These are members of the VRS that I'm referring to. So this quite clearly shows the situation. I don't know what isn't clear. When it comes to the encirclement that I'm talking about, it's not a standard type of encirclement, it's a semi-encirclement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript 62, line 12, the witness said the forward line of defence, not the front line, the forward line of defence of the Serbian forces, the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, isn't it a fact that the SRK and the VRS considered that -- considered the encirclement or the blockade of Sarajevo to be extremely important and that emphasised its maintenance throughout the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: It was extremely important not to allow the forces of the 1st Corps of the ABiH to break through our lines and get out of those positions because they were numerically stronger in terms of troops. So the forces of the 1st Corps would have certainly deployed in other battle-fields with disastrous consequences not only for the SRK but also for Republika Srpska as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me be clear on the question. I presume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First thing, is there a difference, Mr. Simic, between the front line of defence and the forward line of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The forward line of defence concerns units in contact with our forces, with enemy forces. These are units that are in contact. The forward lines of defence in the depth, for example, might mean that only certain positions had been reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And front line of defence, if such a term exists at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not giving evidence, Mr. Karadzic. And if it is not that critical, let's proceed. But since it's raised I'm going to clarify with the witness. Yes, what's the front line of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The front line of defence concerns the positions of our units in contact, in immediate contact, with enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following the difference. But in any event, I'll leave it at that. Shall we give the witness a pen to mark on this map? Could you circle the area when you refer to the internal encirclement of the Serb forces by the Bosnian forces so that we can understand. The area that you referred to as the internally encircled part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see the area here, the Ilidza Brigade, which is here, that's what this means. It's encircled on three sides and there was an opening here for the unit. This area was free in the depth, and you can see that they're in contact here with Miljacka, although the scale of the map is very small, I couldn't tell you which sector this is in. This area here is also encircled, as you can see, as the scale is very small here and it's difficult to make precise markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's ignore the current markings. Can we zoom in a bit further. Once again. Yes. Could you circle again the part which you referred to as internally encircled area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then let's change the colour into blue and could you circle the areas which you referred to as externally encircled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is at the rear. There were the HVO units and the Muslim units in the direction of Kiseljak in the rear, in the direction of Kresevo further on towards Visoko. You can see that the blue line is behind the red one. Our forces are here and Muslim forces are here. And down there you have Muslim forces and our forces again. So this is the internal encirclement and this is the external one, and that was also the case for Trnovo until it was liberated and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you put the today's date, which is 8th of November, and your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you wouldn't mind that we treat this as next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5978, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, notwithstanding these areas that you've pointed out, the fact is, is it not, that the VRS considered that it had Sarajevo encircled and under blockade and constantly emphasised the need to maintain that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The VRS knew that if the 1st Corps broke through in co-operation with other units, if they broke through from the encirclement, 80.000 to 100.000 men would be liberated and put to use on other battle-fields and that would have had disastrous consequences. The Sarajevo Corps might have disappeared -- maybe not, but there would have been a problem with Republika Srpska and who knows where it would have ended. In the course of the entire war the lines weren't moved. The forward line of defence wasn't moved. It was the case that there were movements in certain cases, and in the course of the offensives launched by the Muslim forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, let me -- obviously the answer will not be yes or no so let me just show you a few documents and ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I have D00235, please, and page 3 of the English and can we go to page 2 of the B/C/S. I need page 3 of the English, please. And also page 3 of the B/C/S, please. Okay, it's page 4 -- I'm sorry, I wasn't counting that first correction page, if we can move one page forward for each one. Under "operation objectives" we see for this directive, directive for further operations number 3: "Prevent the breaking of the blockade of Sarajevo ..." And then a few lines down: "Keep Sarajevo firmly under blockade and prevent its breaking." If we can go to 65 ter 11639, page 2, please, of that document. One more -- that's right. And there we see: "Persistent and active defence shall prevent the breaking of the blockade of Sarajevo ..." And it goes on to note: "... while offensive operations shall ensure the liberation of road communications." 65 ter 23834, please. Page 2, please. Item number 8 -- it's still page 1 of the B/C/S, I'm sorry. Item number 8: "Fortify positions around Sarajevo by erecting wire and concrete barriers, which would in turn strengthen the belief that they really are blocked ('in a camp')." And finally P1041, page 2. And page 2 of the B/C/S as well. This is General Mladic speaking: "We have the means and the bridges with which to cross the river. I have blocked Sarajevo from four corners. The city is trapped. There is no way out."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I could show other documents, but isn't it the case that contrary to the suggestion in your statement that it was the VRS or the SRK that was surrounded, that the SRK had Sarajevo encircled, blockaded, and made every effort to maintain that during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have showed you the lines where the VRS units were, where they were encircled, or where they had been semi-encircled, and I showed you the internal and external ring -- were encirclement. I know that area and that part of Sarajevo very well. And the SRK command and if the Main Staff command had ordered someone to let those forces leave, those positions were also defended by inhabitants in the settlements around Sarajevo. So I don't think that anyone would have carried out such an order because what does it mean to leave the entire area, to have significant casualties --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you -- excuse me for interrupting you, but that is not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't it the case, isn't the reality, that contrary to the suggestion in your statement that it was the SRK that was surrounded, that in fact it was the SRK that surrounded Sarajevo, that blockaded Sarajevo, that was known to and emphasised by the Main Staff, and every effort was made to maintain that position during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: It's quite clear that the SRK was encircled as well as the Muslim forces. The area of Sarajevo had an exit in a certain sense and you can see that in the map. It's quite clear why the command of the Main Staff and the corps command issued the orders that they issued; and even if they hadn't issued those orders, a decisive defence would have been mounted and the very last soldier would have put up resistance. It wasn't -- it was the inhabitants of the surrounding settlements who defended their houses, their villages, and they were prepared to defend it. They knew what the consequences were. It wasn't just people who had been brought in from the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to adjourn, but let's put it simple, Mr. Simic. You said "SRK was encircled as well," so you wouldn't deny the ABiH inside the Sarajevo city was also encircled by the SRK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning I said that everyone had -- everyone else in an encirclement, everyone was encircled. What does that mean -- or rather, there was a semi-encirclement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's leave it at that and we'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction in the transcript, please, if I may. The witness said in the previous answer that it was not the army that was brought from elsewhere and those people did very much care whether something would be lost or not, whether an area would fall or not. And also, the witness confirmed His Excellency Kwon's position, he said: Yes, that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue tomorrow at 9.00 -- no, not tomorrow. Monday next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before we rise, Mr. President, I wanted to tender 11639 and 23834.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 11639 will be Exhibit D5979 and 65 ter number 23834 will be Exhibit P5980.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it would be helpful if you could advise the witness that he's not to discuss his testimony during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic, you are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Probably you are aware of this, but do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in the meantime I hope the technical difficulties will be resolved by that time. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of November, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.04 p.m.,
